 Top Stories Editorial | In the event of a minimum wage increase, Pitt needs to support its student workers
 Governor Josh Shapiro speaks at his Pittsburgh campaign rally on Oct. 24, 2026. 
 In the 2026 midterms, Democrats in Pennsylvania won a rare “trifecta,” controlling the gubernatorial seat and both chambers of state legislature. Having achieved this, Governor Josh Shapiro vows that the first bill he will sign into law in January is a minimum wage increase from $7.25 to $15.  
 While this increase will largely benefit Pennsylvania as one of the 20 states which has stuck to the federal minimum wage since 2009, it poses a potential threat to jobs that currently don’t receive enough funding to meet that minimum wage, especially at universities. The Republicans of the Pennsylvania state legislature likely didn’t realize they were protecting The Pitt News editorial board when they blocked past efforts to raise the minimum wage, but they were.  
 The Pitt News employees are not the only student employees making below the proposed increase to the minimum wage. The minimum wage at Pitt for student workers is $10 an hour — an increase from $7.25 that occurred only last year — and many departments cannot afford to pay more. Student employment is essential, creating opportunities for students to gain work experience and develop their resumes while providing an income that can help them prepare for their future and pay for their education. 
 Pitt’s administration must prepare now to support student workers rather than cutting pay or cutting positions entirely, in the likely case of a $15 minimum wage. They cannot plead unpreparedness, and student success is on the line.  
 The Pitt News editorial is written by the opinion editors in collaboration with other desk editors. It reflects the collective opinion of the current Pitt News editorial staff.
